title: Mechanistic Interpretability Tinkering
text:
Informal notes from tinkering with the internals of language models.









A month of poking at plans: two things that held up, eight that didn’t


I wanted to watch a plan form and dissolve inside a model as it writes. Dissolution turned out not to be a thing. But the plan does get read — late, and barely.





Aug 27, 2026







Looped transformers solve S5 by re-deriving, not by carrying state


I hoped forcing recurrence would make a transformer carry a running state. It length-generalizes better — but a causal swap says it’s still re-deriving every step. And getting even that to happen reliably is its own puzzle.





Jul 12, 2026







Function vectors don’t make it through natural-language autoencoders


I was interested whether we could see the effect of function vectors on NLA verbalizations. Looks like we can’t.

title: A month of poking at plans: two things that held up, eight that didn’t
text:
There’s a nice result from the poetry-planning work where a model writing a rhyming couplet seems to pick the rhyme word early — it’s sitting there in the representation at the line break, before the model has written the line that leads up to it. Ma & Rui localized that pretty precisely, and then said something I found irresistible: patching shows the plan is encoded there, but it can’t tell you whether the model ever actually reads it.
So that was the question. And I wanted the fuller version: if a plan forms, presumably it also gets used and then goes away. Formation, persistence, dissolution. Watch the whole lifecycle.
Everything ran locally on a laptop (gemma-2-9b-it), no training, total spend $0.

title: A month of poking at plans: two things that held up, eight that didn’t
section: The tool: blocking attention, but only for some queries
text:
The tool: blocking attention, but only for some queries
The trick that made this work: instead of ablating a position, I block attention from a chosen set of query positions to a chosen set of key positions. So I can let the prompt’s own forward pass see the newline normally, and only starve the later positions of it.
That difference is the whole measurement. If blocking a source for everyone hurts but blocking it only for late positions doesn’t, the information was extracted early and cached. If starving the late positions hurts, it’s being read at that moment. It time-stamps when something was consulted.

title: A month of poking at plans: two things that held up, eight that didn’t
section: Thing 1: the plan gets read, and the rhyme word doesn’t
text:
Thing 1: the plan gets read, and the rhyme word doesn’t
Blocking line two’s access to the comma-and-newline at the end of line one costs 1.47 nats on the eventual rhyme word (n=37). The newline by itself costs 0.64. A matched content word from the same line costs nothing (+0.06). So it’s specifically the boundary, not “line one” in general.
Now the fun part. Blocking the actual rhyme word of line one — the thing the second line has to rhyme with — costs nothing at all (+0.03, not significant). The model isn’t looking back at the word it needs to rhyme with. It’s looking at the boundary where it stashed its decision.
And it reads late. Nothing at all 9 tokens out. Dependence shows up in the last ~6 tokens, peaks around 3 tokens before the word is due. Also it barely needs the channel — scale that attention down to 10% and the cost mostly vanishes (0.04 nats).
So: written early, read just-in-time, through a narrow pipe.

title: A month of poking at plans: two things that held up, eight that didn’t
section: Thing 2: the model reads its own reasoning, not the question
text:
Thing 2: the model reads its own reasoning, not the question
Different substrate, same tool. Arithmetic word problems the model gets right 15% of the time in one shot and 100% of the time with a chain of thought.
Take the successful runs and make the trace write-only — the tokens are all still there, literally not one character changed, but the final answer position can’t attend to them. Accuracy goes 1.00 → 0.00, twenty for twenty. Matched control condition: 1.00. Fine, expected.
The bit I liked: block the question instead and accuracy stays at 1.00, all twenty. Once the trace exists the model has stopped consulting the problem statement. The reasoning has superseded its own input.
And it’s not just copying the answer out of its own scratchpad — that was my first suspicion. The answer’s digits literally appear in the trace, so maybe the model is just reading them off. Block only those occurrences: costs 0.001 nats and preserves the argmax on all 20. Block the trace minus those occurrences: 1.68 nats and 80% of the answers break. It’s using the reasoning, not the number.

title: A month of poking at plans: two things that held up, eight that didn’t
text:
The eight that didn’t work
I set out with a bunch of ambitious hypotheses. Eight of nine died, mostly to controls I ran myself, which is the system working but is also a lot of dead ends:

Dissolution isn’t a thing (the premise!). Plans don’t terminate, they get released and re-activated as they become relevant again. 71/71 poems.
Provenance — does it matter if the model chose the constraint vs. was given it? No; the self-generated case was the most source-dependent, opposite of the prediction.
Compressibility — no gradient at all.
A “slot” hypothesis about tokenization and boundaries — pilot looked great at n≈10, died in all three models when properly powered.
Prose redundancy, threshold-reading, margin-as-object, mechanistic unfaithfulness detection — all killed, mostly by powered replications of my own underpowered pilots.

Pattern I can’t ignore: the two things that survived were both me answering somebody else’s explicitly stated open question. The eight corpses were all my own clever ideas.

title: A month of poking at plans: two things that held up, eight that didn’t
section: What I’d actually tell someone doing this
text:
What I’d actually tell someone doing this
Honestly this might be the useful part of the whole month:

Attention mass does not tell you what matters causally — and whether it does is model-dependent. Top-5 heads by attention mass were 1% of the effect on the 2B model (the causally important heads ranked 6th and 8th). On the 9B, top-10 were 95%. Same method, opposite conclusion. Everybody publishes the success case.
Readable ≠ used, and unreadable ≠ unused. I had a constraint that was causally decisive while being invisible to the lens, and separately a readout I could degrade to nothing with zero behavioral effect. A probe can be wrong in both directions.
Binary ablation and graded attenuation tell different stories. I confidently had a “knife-edge” result — flat until 15% bandwidth, then a cliff — which dissolved into a boring gradual decline once I ran a finer grid.
With a continuous DV you can get p=1e-06 on a difference of 0.001 nats. Effect size is the only endpoint worth reporting.
Two silent bugs each would have inverted a conclusion, both caught by controls rather than by me being clever. One was a torch/MPS dtype-conversion returning all zeros, so an entire causal run was a no-op that looked like a clean null.

title: A month of poking at plans: two things that held up, eight that didn’t
text:
Why I’m stopping
The instrument works and I like the two results, but a 9B model with hand-built tasks on one laptop bounds how big a finding is available, and I don’t think this line has a big one in it. Setting it down.
The one thing I’d want if I picked it back up: a boundary-specificity control on Thing 1. My control rules out generic content dependence but not generic boundary dependence — a mid-line comma, or the same boundary in a task with no rhyme to plan. Cheap, and it’s the claim most exposed to a confound.

title: A month of poking at plans: two things that held up, eight that didn’t
text:
Caveats
One model, one seed of each task, n=37 and n=20. Thing 1 is a nearby model to Ma & Rui’s rather than theirs (their result is on Gemma-3-27B, which doesn’t fit on my laptop), so treat it as an independent instrument agreeing rather than a replication. Everything is teacher-forced at a chosen readout position, not free generation.

title: Looped transformers solve S5 by re-deriving, not by carrying state
text:
Beginning to work on a longer-term project to try and identify slices of a circuit that operate on spans larger than a single token. As a starting point, I wanted to study a simplified toy model capable of the cleanest version of that: tracking a running state across a sequence. Permutation composition on S₅ is a nice fit — you’re handed a sequence of permutations and have to report the running composition after each one — because it forces a genuine span-level computation and there’s a sharp distinction between two ways to do it.
You can carry a running state and update it each step (the “real” span-level algorithm — the thing I ultimately want to find circuits for), or you can re-derive the state at each position from scratch by looking back over all the raw actions (a shortcut that happens to work). Which one a model actually does is exactly the kind of question the broader project is about, and S₅ lets me ask it in a setting clean enough to answer causally.
The goal is a model that solves the task the way you’re supposed to: hold a running state and update it each step. That carried state is the span-level computation I want to study, so I need a model that genuinely builds one — not one that fakes the answer with a lookback shortcut.
Plain transformers can learn to do this — Li et al. show they’ll sometimes find the proper carry-style algorithm and length-generalize impressively far. The catch is that they find it unreliably: whether a given training run lands on the genuine algorithm or on a brittle shortcut that breaks past the training length seems to come down to the luck of initialization and data order.
My hope was that a looped transformer — a weight-tied block repeated more times for longer inputs, à la Fan et al. — would make the carry solution the default rather than a lucky draw, by handing the model depth that scales with the input the way a genuine step-by-step computation would need. But this turned out to just provide the model with the extra depth it needed to better execute the shortcut computational approach — re-deriving the state more effectively — without ever learning the carried state.

title: Looped transformers solve S5 by re-deriving, not by carrying state
text:
What I actually did (in order)
First, just try to reproduce Li. I trained a plain Pythia-160M on the S₅ task the way the paper describes and gated it for length generalization. It learned to track — but only shallowly, holding up to about depth 9–12 before falling apart, nowhere near the numbers the paper reports (up to ~106). So: a genuine tracker, but a weak one, and not the reliable long-range carry I was after.
Maybe it was the seed. Li is explicit that the good algorithm is a lottery of initialization and data order — they report proportions over as many as 20 replicates. So I ran a few more seeds. They all clustered in the same 9–12 band. No seed broke out into the deep-generalizing regime; the variation was in shallow tracking depth, not in whether it generalized at all.
Was the training even trending the right way? Before sinking a full multi-day sweep into seed-hunting, I ran a couple of truncated runs and looked at the early mechanism signature — was anything heading toward the good solution given more time? Nothing obviously was. The runs looked like they were settling into the same shallow shortcut, not slowly grokking their way toward carry.
So I pivoted. Between the flat seed results and a limited compute budget, chasing a lucky plain-transformer run looked like a bad bet. The more interesting question was whether a different architecture would exhibit the carry behavior more reliably — which is what took me to the looped transformer.

title: Looped transformers solve S5 by re-deriving, not by carrying state
section: The looped model generalizes better — but not reliably
text:
The looped model generalizes better — but not reliably
A 4-layer looped block does length-generalize on S₅ where the plain transformer capped out. Trained to length 24, it stays near-perfect out to ~depth 30 and degrades gracefully past that — clearly beating the ~9–12 ceiling I kept hitting with the vanilla model.
But here’s the first surprise: it only happens on about 2 of 3 seeds. Same architecture, same data, same recipe — two seeds generalize cleanly (cutoff ~25, ~0.98 accuracy); the third lands in a failing regime and never gets off the ground (~chance). This mirrors the lottery Li describes for plain transformers — the mechanism you get is partly luck of init and data order — except looping seems to raise the odds rather than remove the lottery.

title: Looped transformers solve S5 by re-deriving, not by carrying state
section: The causal test: it’s re-deriving, not carrying
text:
The causal test: it’s re-deriving, not carrying
For the seeds that do generalize, I ran a directed counterfactual swap. The idea: at some position, overwrite the model’s internal running state with a different valid state (a class-mean translation in the residual stream — an on-manifold edit), then watch what happens downstream.

If the model carries state, corrupting it at position p should corrupt everything after p — the wrong state propagates forward.
If the model re-derives, downstream positions recompute the correct state from the raw actions and shrug off the swap.

The result was unambiguous:

At the swapped position: the edit takes — the model reports the counterfactual state (~99%).
One or more positions downstream: the model reports the correct original state ~100% of the time. The perturbation does not propagate at all.

That’s the re-derive signature — the same one the plain model shows.
I also probed along the loop-iteration axis, and it tells a consistent story: the state at a position is built up progressively across loop iterations (undecodable for the first few iterations, then snapping in around iteration 4–6). So the recurrence is doing real sequential computation — it’s just spending that computation re-deriving each position to more depth, not threading a running state across positions.
So the mechanism is something like “parallel-per-position, deepened-by-iteration.” Looping buys a higher length-generalization ceiling by giving each position more effective depth to re-derive with — not by teaching the model to carry.

title: Looped transformers solve S5 by re-deriving, not by carrying state
text:
Checking I didn’t fool myself
A no-propagation result is easy to get for boring reasons — swapped at the wrong spot, swapped too late, one lucky sequence — so I swept it:

Position: swapped at positions 2, 6, and 10 — identical re-derive signature at all three.
Timing: injected the perturbation both late (final loop iteration) and early (iteration 4, right as the state first becomes decodable) — still no downstream propagation either way.
Seeds: both generalizing seeds give near-identical numbers.
The failing seed never tracks well enough for the analysis to have anything to bite on — which is itself a check that the tooling isn’t manufacturing signal.

The one thing I haven’t fully pinned down: my counterfactual edit is a class-mean translation, and I’d want to confirm that operator is a faithful stand-in for the model’s real state-direction before leaning too hard on the quantitative claim. Treat the numbers as strong-but-preliminary.

title: Looped transformers solve S5 by re-deriving, not by carrying state
text:
Where this leaves me
Two tentative takeaways:

Even an architecture built for recurrence didn’t discover the carry algorithm. It found a better re-derivation instead. If carry is what you want, looping alone may not get you there — the natural follow-up is architectures with genuine sequential state (DeltaNet / DeltaProduct-style linear-attention variants), the one family theorized to actually carry.
Reliability is the sharper question. The fact that the “good” solution only shows up ~2/3 of the time — and that this seems to be a property of the optimization, not just the architecture — is the thread I find most worth pulling. What makes a training run land in the generalizing basin versus the failing one?

This is very much tinkering-in-progress, and I’m not convinced I won’t come back to it — getting reliable carry to actually occur feels like a genuinely interesting research question, not just an engineering nuisance.

title: Function vectors don’t make it through natural-language autoencoders
text: I was interested in seeing whether NLAs could be used to understand function vectors, with the potentially broader goal of using NLAs to enable the creation of more general FVs than currently exist in the literature — which are limited to fairly concrete, mechanical operations, with not much in the way of higher-level FVs. But after applying an FV, neither the NLA verbalization nor the AR re-embedding preserved the effect of the FV.

title: Function vectors don’t make it through natural-language autoencoders
text: I was interested in seeing whether NLAs could be used to understand function vectors, with the potentially broader goal of using NLAs to enable the creation of more general FVs than currently exist in the literature — which are limited to fairly concrete, mechanical operations, with not much in the way of higher-level FVs. But after applying an FV, neither the NLA verbalization nor the AR re-embedding preserved the effect of the FV.

title: Function vectors don’t make it through natural-language autoencoders
text:
Setup (the short version)
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on a laptop, forward-pass only, no training. The NLA is Anthropic’s released Qwen checkpoint pair that reads/writes the layer-20 residual stream. The function vector is for the country→capital task, extracted with Todd et al.’s method. To avoid eyeballing paragraphs, I score a verbalization by reconstructing it back to a vector and measuring cosine similarity to a “country→capital” target vector — higher means the verbalization’s meaning is nearer “country→capital.” (The reconstructor is itself lossy, so this metric isn’t ground truth — which is why the controls below matter.)

title: Function vectors don’t make it through natural-language autoencoders
section: Step 1: the FV steers (the write side works)
text:
Step 1: the FV steers (the write side works)
Add the country→capital FV at layer 17 of a zero-shot Q: <country>\nA: prompt and look at the next token:

Q: France\nA: → “Paris” enters the top-3 (9.1%) only with the FV, absent from the clean run.
Q: Japan\nA: → “Tokyo” enters the top-3 (5.5%) only with the FV.

Modest — this is 7B zero-shot, not the ideal in-context setup — but unambiguous. The write side works.

title: Function vectors don’t make it through natural-language autoencoders
section: Step 2: the FV does not verbalize (the read side fails)
text:
Step 2: the FV does not verbalize (the read side fails)
Two ways to read it, both fail:
(a) Verbalize the raw FV. Feed it straight to the verbalizer → incoherent stuff about “structured math / TensorFlow / the number 15.” No geography. Unsurprising in hindsight: a raw FV is a sum of head outputs, not a state the model actually occupies, so it’s off-distribution for a verbalizer trained on real activations.
(b) Verbalize the FV’s effect. The principled version: add the FV during a forward pass and verbalize the actual layer-20 state it produces (a real, on-distribution activation, just nudged). At first this looked like it worked — the FV-steered Q: France\nA: verbalized as “…what is the capital of…trivia about a country…”.
But that was prompt leakage — the prompt already said “France.” Redo it on neutral prompts with no geography ("The answer is", "I think that", "It is") and the country/capital signal vanishes. With and without the FV, the verbalizations are basically identical, and neither mentions countries or capitals.

title: Function vectors don’t make it through natural-language autoencoders
text:
Step 3: verifying the negative
A null only means something if the instrument can detect a true positive and you pushed the intervention hard enough. Two controls:

Positive control: score real country→capital states (the layer-20 activation at the answer position of “The capital of France is”) vs. clearly-unrelated states (2+2=, python code, “once upon a time”).
Strong injection: re-run (b) at injection strengths ×1, ×3, ×5, ×8. At ×8 the state is heavily perturbed (cosine to clean drops to 0.62), so this is not a timid nudge.

Everything on one axis:



Function-vector-injected states verbalize like unrelated states, not like real country→capital states — even at 8× injection.



Real capital states: ~0.76. The metric lights up; the verbalizer even describes them as “a famous city in Japan… what is the capital of…”. The instrument is not blind.
Unrelated states: ~0.55.
FV-injected states: ~0.54, flat from ×1 to ×8. They sit in the unrelated band and never move toward the capital band, even when the injection nearly breaks the state.

So the null in Step 2 is real — not a dead metric, not a too-gentle nudge.

title: Function vectors don’t make it through natural-language autoencoders
text:
Caveats
I tried one task, one model, and one FV. Hardly thorough, but enough to get me to move on to other things.
